# Random Forest for Classification

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical foundations of bootstrap sampling, ensembles, and Random Forest are developed in Chapters 7 and 14 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- explain how Random Forest combines many decision trees;
- distinguish bootstrap sampling, random predictor selection, and aggregation;
- interpret the roles of `num.trees`, `mtry`, and `min.node.size`;
- use out-of-bag (OOB) error to support model development without touching the final test set;
- interpret the OOB Brier score of a probability forest;
- distinguish impurity-based and permutation importance;
- evaluate a forest using a confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy;
- apply the method to ATUS and an educational COVID-19 route.

## Core idea

Random Forest constructs many partially different trees and aggregates their predictions [@breiman2001random]. For classification, the final decision can be represented as

$$
\widehat y(x)=\operatorname{mode}
\left\{
\widehat y^{(1)}(x),\ldots,\widehat y^{(B)}(x)
\right\}.
$$

Two mechanisms create diversity among trees:

1. each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample from the training data;
2. at each split, only a random subset of predictors is considered.

Reducing correlation among trees and averaging many decisions generally makes the forest more stable than a single decision tree.

## Out-of-bag observations

An observation not selected in a tree's bootstrap sample is **out-of-bag** for that tree. OOB predictions provide an internal way to estimate performance using observations that were not used to grow the corresponding trees.

::: {.callout-important title="OOB does not necessarily replace a final test set"}
OOB error is extremely useful for model development and hyperparameter comparison within the training data. If an independent test set has been reserved, it should remain untouched for final external evaluation.
:::

With `ranger`, when `probability = TRUE`, `prediction.error` is the **OOB Brier score**. For a binary event,

$$
BS=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(p_i-y_i)^2,
$$

where smaller values indicate better probability predictions in squared-error terms.

## Helper functions

```{r random-forest-helpers-en}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ranger)
source("../util_graficas.R")

stratified_rf_split <- function(y, prop_train = 0.80, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  y <- factor(y)
  idx_train <- integer(0)

  for (class_value in levels(y)) {
    ids <- sample(which(y == class_value))
    n_train <- floor(prop_train * length(ids))
    idx_train <- c(idx_train, ids[seq_len(n_train)])
  }

  idx_train <- sort(idx_train)
  list(
    train = idx_train,
    test = setdiff(seq_along(y), idx_train)
  )
}

rf_metrics <- function(actual, predicted, positive, negative) {
  actual <- factor(actual, levels = c(positive, negative))
  predicted <- factor(predicted, levels = c(positive, negative))
  m <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)

  TP <- m[positive, positive]
  FN <- m[positive, negative]
  FP <- m[negative, positive]
  TN <- m[negative, negative]

  safe_divide <- function(a, b) if (b == 0) NA_real_ else a / b
  sensitivity <- safe_divide(TP, TP + FN)
  specificity <- safe_divide(TN, TN + FP)

  list(
    confusion = m,
    metrics = data.frame(
      accuracy = safe_divide(TP + TN, sum(m)),
      sensitivity = sensitivity,
      specificity = specificity,
      balanced_accuracy = mean(c(sensitivity, specificity), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
}
```

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Load and prepare a reproducible sample

```{r prepare-rf-atus-en}
atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (!file.exists(atus_path)) {
  stop("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run Chapter 2 first.")
}

atus_ml <- read_csv(atus_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

set.seed(2026)
atus_rf_base <- atus_ml |>
  mutate(
    accident_class = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños"),
      labels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
    ),
    MES = as.factor(MES),
    HOUR_NUM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ID_HORA)),
    HOUR_NUM = ifelse(
      HOUR_NUM >= 0 & HOUR_NUM <= 23,
      HOUR_NUM,
      NA_real_
    ),
    DIASEMANA = as.factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = as.factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = as.factor(CAUSAACCI)
  ) |>
  drop_na(
    accident_class,
    MES,
    HOUR_NUM,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  ) |>
  slice_sample(n = min(15000, n()))

data.frame(
  rows = nrow(atus_rf_base),
  columns = ncol(atus_rf_base)
)
```

```{r rf-class-distribution-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(
  atus_rf_base,
  aes(x = accident_class, fill = accident_class)
) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.7) +
  escala_clases_fill() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = etiqueta_numero) +
  labs(
    title = "Response-class distribution",
    subtitle = "Working sample for Random Forest",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Number of accidents"
  ) +
  tema_libro() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Stratified training-test split

```{r split-rf-atus-en}
parts_atus <- stratified_rf_split(
  atus_rf_base$accident_class,
  prop_train = 0.80,
  seed = 2026
)

train <- atus_rf_base[parts_atus$train, ]
test <- atus_rf_base[parts_atus$test, ]

rbind(
  training = prop.table(table(train$accident_class)),
  test = prop.table(table(test$accident_class))
)
```

## Select mtry using OOB Brier score

With five predictors, several values of `mtry` are compared inside the training data. The test set remains untouched.

```{r select-mtry-rf-atus-en}
rf_formula <- accident_class ~
  MES + HOUR_NUM + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI

mtry_values <- 1:5

mtry_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(mtry_values, function(current_mtry) {
    set.seed(2026 + current_mtry)

    model <- ranger(
      rf_formula,
      data = train,
      num.trees = 150,
      mtry = current_mtry,
      min.node.size = 20,
      probability = TRUE,
      importance = "none",
      seed = 2026 + current_mtry
    )

    data.frame(
      mtry = current_mtry,
      oob_brier = model$prediction.error
    )
  })
)

mtry_results

best_mtry <- mtry_results$mtry[
  which.min(mtry_results$oob_brier)
]

best_mtry
```

```{r plot-mtry-rf-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(mtry_results, aes(x = mtry, y = oob_brier)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = col_azul) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = col_coral) +
  labs(
    title = "Selecting mtry using OOB Brier score",
    subtitle = "Smaller values indicate better OOB probabilistic performance",
    x = "mtry",
    y = "OOB Brier score"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

## Fit the final forest

```{r fit-final-rf-atus-en}
set.seed(2026)

model_rf <- ranger(
  rf_formula,
  data = train,
  num.trees = 300,
  mtry = best_mtry,
  min.node.size = 20,
  importance = "permutation",
  probability = TRUE,
  seed = 2026
)

model_rf
```

::: {.callout-note title="How many trees?"}
Increasing `num.trees` usually stabilizes predictions, but improvements eventually become small while computational cost continues to increase. There is no universally optimal number; stability and computation time should both be considered.
:::

## Permutation importance

```{r permutation-importance-rf-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
importance_rf <- data.frame(
  variable = names(model_rf$variable.importance),
  importance = as.numeric(model_rf$variable.importance)
) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

importance_rf

ggplot(
  importance_rf,
  aes(x = reorder(variable, importance), y = importance)
) +
  geom_col(fill = col_azul, width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Permutation importance in Random Forest",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Importance"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Importance is not causation"}
Permutation importance describes how predictive performance deteriorates when a predictor is disrupted. It does not establish causality and can be shared among correlated predictors.
:::

## Final evaluation on the test set

```{r evaluate-rf-atus-en}
rf_predictions <- predict(
  model_rf,
  data = test
)$predictions

prob_victims <- rf_predictions[, "With casualties"]

class_rf <- colnames(rf_predictions)[
  max.col(rf_predictions, ties.method = "first")
]

result_rf <- rf_metrics(
  test$accident_class,
  class_rf,
  positive = "With casualties",
  negative = "Property damage only"
)

result_rf$confusion
result_rf$metrics
```

## Distribution of predicted probabilities

```{r rf-probabilities-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
rf_probability_data <- data.frame(
  probability = prob_victims,
  actual_class = test$accident_class
)

ggplot(
  rf_probability_data,
  aes(x = probability, fill = actual_class)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.65, position = "identity") +
  escala_clases_fill(name = "Actual class") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of predicted probabilities",
    subtitle = "Random Forest",
    x = "Predicted probability of 'With casualties'",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Probability and class are different outputs"}
A probability forest returns class probabilities. A class label requires a decision rule; here we choose the class with the larger probability. When false positives and false negatives have different costs, a threshold should be selected and validated explicitly.
:::

# Interactive laboratory: forest voting

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
This simulator shows how multiple trees vote and how the cumulative vote proportion tends to stabilize as the number of trees increases.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 700
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Random Forest voting simulator"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("ntree", "Number of trees", 5, 200, 50, step = 5),
      sliderInput(
        "prob",
        "Probability that one tree votes for Class 1",
        0.05, 0.95, 0.65, step = 0.05
      ),
      numericInput("seed", "Seed", 123, min = 1),
      actionButton("simulate", "Simulate forest")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("votes", height = "360px"),
      tableOutput("summary"),
      textOutput("prediction")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  data_sim <- eventReactive(input$simulate, {
    set.seed(input$seed)
    votes <- rbinom(input$ntree, 1, input$prob)
    data.frame(
      tree = seq_along(votes),
      vote = votes,
      cumulative = cumsum(votes) / seq_along(votes)
    )
  }, ignoreNULL = FALSE)

  output$votes <- renderPlot({
    d <- data_sim()
    plot(
      d$tree,
      d$cumulative,
      type = "l",
      lwd = 3,
      ylim = c(0, 1),
      xlab = "Cumulative number of trees",
      ylab = "Cumulative proportion of Class 1 votes",
      main = "Stabilization of forest voting"
    )
    abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)
    grid()
  })

  output$summary <- renderTable({
    d <- data_sim()
    votes1 <- sum(d$vote == 1)
    votes0 <- sum(d$vote == 0)
    data.frame(
      Class = c("Class 0", "Class 1"),
      Votes = c(votes0, votes1),
      Percentage = round(100 * c(votes0, votes1) / nrow(d), 1)
    )
  })

  output$prediction <- renderText({
    d <- data_sim()
    predicted_class <- ifelse(mean(d$vote) >= 0.5, "Class 1", "Class 0")
    paste("Final forest prediction:", predicted_class)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
### Laboratory available in the web edition
The laboratory allows the reader to change the number of trees and observe how the cumulative vote proportion stabilizes.
:::

# Applied Case B: Random Forest with COVID-19

## Select the period reproducibly

```{r select-covid-rf-en}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(ESTADO == "PROCESADO", !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)) |>
  slice_max(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", covid_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  stop("The COVID-19 dataset selected by the reproducible procedure was not found.")
}
```

## Prepare and split the sample

```{r prepare-covid-rf-en}
covid_rf <- read_csv(covid_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(
      MURIO,
      levels = c(1, 0),
      labels = c("Recorded death", "No recorded death")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-MURIO)

set.seed(2026)
covid_rf <- covid_rf |>
  slice_sample(n = min(10000, n()))

parts_covid <- stratified_rf_split(
  covid_rf$outcome,
  prop_train = 0.80,
  seed = 2026
)

covid_train <- covid_rf[parts_covid$train, ]
covid_test <- covid_rf[parts_covid$test, ]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
Importance scores and probabilities come from an administrative sample prepared for teaching. They do not constitute a clinical diagnostic or prognostic model, and if prevalence was modified, raw probabilities do not represent population risk.
:::

## Select mtry with OOB Brier score and fit the final forest

```{r select-mtry-covid-rf-en}
covid_rf_formula <- outcome ~
  EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES + HIPERTENSION +
  OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA + NUM_COMORBILIDADES

mtry_candidates <- 2:5

covid_mtry_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(mtry_candidates, function(current_mtry) {
    model <- ranger(
      covid_rf_formula,
      data = covid_train,
      num.trees = 150,
      mtry = current_mtry,
      min.node.size = 20,
      probability = TRUE,
      importance = "none",
      seed = 2026 + current_mtry
    )

    data.frame(
      mtry = current_mtry,
      oob_brier = model$prediction.error
    )
  })
)

best_mtry_covid <- covid_mtry_results$mtry[
  which.min(covid_mtry_results$oob_brier)
]

covid_mtry_results
best_mtry_covid
```

```{r final-covid-rf-model-en}
covid_rf_model <- ranger(
  covid_rf_formula,
  data = covid_train,
  num.trees = 300,
  mtry = best_mtry_covid,
  min.node.size = 20,
  probability = TRUE,
  importance = "permutation",
  seed = 2026
)

covid_rf_model
```

## COVID-19 importance and final evaluation

```{r importance-covid-rf-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
covid_importance <- data.frame(
  variable = names(covid_rf_model$variable.importance),
  importance = as.numeric(covid_rf_model$variable.importance)
) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

covid_importance

ggplot(
  covid_importance,
  aes(x = reorder(variable, importance), y = importance)
) +
  geom_col(fill = col_azul, width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Permutation importance: COVID-19 Random Forest",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Importance"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

```{r metrics-covid-rf-en}
covid_probabilities <- predict(
  covid_rf_model,
  data = covid_test
)$predictions

covid_classes <- colnames(covid_probabilities)[
  max.col(covid_probabilities, ties.method = "first")
]

result_covid_rf <- rf_metrics(
  covid_test$outcome,
  covid_classes,
  positive = "Recorded death",
  negative = "No recorded death"
)

result_covid_rf$confusion
result_covid_rf$metrics
```

## Chapter summary

Random Forest reduces the instability of a single tree by combining bootstrap resampling, random predictor selection, and aggregation. OOB error supports model development within the training data, while an external test set provides independent final evaluation. Variable importance and predicted probabilities are useful, but they require careful interpretation and should not be confused with causality or automatically calibrated population risk.

## Fundamental references

Random Forest was formalized by @breiman2001random. A didactic statistical-learning treatment can also be found in @james2021islr.
